# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters.
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:

         git push origin main
         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
         git push origin main:blinded-fable

     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## The library's arrays and algebra

FACTS.md:219
- F-264 **In the interpreter's library, nine `Vector` and `Matrix` operators and three branches of the array factories get their declared type through the function `cast`, and so does the sub-array that `Array2`'s column and row subscripts pass to `Col` and `Row`.** `cast[\T\](x)` returns `x` if it has type `T`, and raises `CastError` if not (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:33-37`). The operators are `Vector`'s `+`, binary and unary `-`, `scale` and `pmul`, and `Matrix`'s `+`, binary and unary `-` and `scale`. Each builds its result with the inherited `map` or `ivmap`, typed `Array1` or `Array2`, and so through `replica`, the method that makes an array of the same layout. The factory branches are those of `__builtinFactory1`, `__immutableFactory1` and `__builtinFactory2` for an array whose lowest indices are 0, each cast to its factory's declared result type. The subscripts are `a[:, j]` and `a[i, :]`. Each builds its sub-array with a range subscript, which answers an unsized `Array`, and the cast gives it the sized `Array2` that the field of `Col` or `Row` takes. Five bodies build with `fill` or `tabulate` and need no cast, since `Vector` and `Matrix` redeclare those two at their own type (F-158): the factories `vector(v)`, `tabulatedVector` and `matrix(v)`, and `Matrix`'s `rmul` and `lmul`. So the compiled checker accepts all these bodies (the distance stage). Under walk each cast holds at the eight number types (`tests/VectorMatrixCastsWalk.fss`). ## Natives

The library binds each of walk's natives by a declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The string names one of these:

- A glue class, as `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X`, in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. A glue class takes the evaluator's boxed values, so the compiled path cannot use it. Most bindings name one.
- A helper: a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, as `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.<method>`. `glue/StaticNativeApp.java` calls it by reflection, with a method's `self` first. The compiled path calls it too (`compiler.md`, "Natives").

Walk carries each declared type of a helper's binding in one Java type:

- `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `Char` in `int`; `ZZ64` and `NN64` in `long`; `RR64` in `double`; `RR32` in `float`; `Boolean` in `boolean`;
- `String`, `FlatString` and `JavaString` in `String`; `ZZ` in `BigInteger`; `()` in `void`.

Walk refuses a helper's binding at load in these cases. The message names the string, and contains the words below, which a `load_exception_contains` key can match:

- The class or the method does not exist: 'not found' or 'names no static method of'.
- The result type, or a parameter type other than `self`'s, is not in the list above: 'no Java type carries the declared'.
- No method of that name, or more than one, has exactly the Java types of the list: 'has no overload that fits the declaration's types', or 'overloads that fit'.

Walk does not check `self`. It passes `self` as the helper's first Java parameter, read as that parameter's Java type. So a binding in a method of a program's own type loads, and a `String` parameter receives the type's name (ledger row 847). Bind a helper in a method only if the helper's first Java parameter carries the type of `self`, as `int` for a method of `ZZ32`.

A native declared over `String`, glue class or helper alike, receives the wrong text for a `CatString`: the name of the type, not its characters (ledger row 846). `||` builds a `CatString` when the joined string is longer than `maxLeafSize`, 32 characters by default. If a string that reaches such a native can come from `||`, pass it as `s.asFlatString` at the call of the native.

An `import java` written in a `.fss` file is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it. The compiled path's generated `import java` (`compiler.md`, "Natives") is not this one.

A glue class raises a Fortress exception that a `catch` sees by throwing a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `Int.overflow()` in `Int.java` there makes one, and its callers throw it:

    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
    return new FortressError(f);

A helper runs on both paths, so it raises an exception as compiled code does: `throw Utility.makeFortressException("fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero")` (`compiler/runtimeValues/Utility.java`). The string names the compiler's prelude's class for the exception. Under walk, that class does not load, and `StaticNativeApp` raises the interpreter's library's object of the same name in its place. So raise from a helper only an exception that both libraries declare as an object, as `DivisionByZero` and `IntegerOverflow`. `ZZ32`'s `DIV` by zero raises `DivisionByZero` in this way. A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other exception from a native ends the run, as a division by zero in a glue class does.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/cloud-container

# The cloud container

**container**
: Virtual machine with its own disk, on which a cloud session of Claude Code runs. It holds a clone of the branch that the session was created from.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**main session**
: Top-level session of a container, which the curator talks to. The agents that it launches are not main sessions.

**coordinating session**
: Main session that keeps the project's files under `explorations/coordinator/` and launches the workers.

**process stop**
: End of the session's Claude Code process, by the platform's cap, by idleness or by a VM restart. The platform starts the process again in the same session.

**VM restart**
: Restart of the container's machine under a live session.

**check-in**
: One-shot reminder, armed with `send_later`, that wakes the main session with a message at a set time.

**Stop hook**
: Command that Claude Code runs at the end of every turn of the main session.

The platform stops the session's process about every 13 hours and when the session goes idle. It can restart the VM, sometimes with the disk rolled back, and it can lose the container. Running agents survive none of these.

## Rules for every agent

- Before a long run, read the room left on the disk as `references/machine.md` says.
- If your brief lets you push, push your work as you go, as `fortress-repo`'s `references/committing.md` says. Only what is pushed survives a rollback of the disk or a lost container.
- After a process stop, a VM restart or a lost container, run `git status` and `git log origin/<branch>..<branch>` in each tree that you work in, before you start anything again.
- The platform's git-check Stop hook can still ask the main session to commit and push on a turn that the git-check switch misses (`references/hooks.md`). Treat its reminders as advisory. Never commit or push unready work to answer one.

## The parts

- `references/machine.md`, for every agent: the machine, timings across sessions, agents at once, the disk allowance and a full disk, the blocked hosts.
- `references/stops.md`, for every agent: the kinds of process stop and their signs, a disk rolled back, the weekly usage limit, what a stop keeps here. Its section on check-ins is for the coordinating session.
- `references/hooks.md`, for the coordinating session: the transcript backup and its blind spots, the git-check hook and how it is turned off.
- `references/container-loss.md`, for the coordinating session: re-provisioning, re-arming the backup, reading another session's transcript, recovering the work.

How a Claude Code session behaves anywhere (the Bash tool, long commands, waits and the prompt cache, interrupts, the automatic permission check) is `fortress-repo`'s `references/session.md`. Running agents and resuming a run are the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`.

`references/sources.md` gives the source of each fact in these parts. Use it only to maintain this skill. Do not load it for a task.

content.content:
## The disk allowance

`df -h /` misleads. Its Size column is the whole disk, about 250 GB, and most of it is reserved and cannot be written. The session may use Used plus Avail, about 37 GB, and Use% is taken of that sum. Read the Avail column: it is what is left.

- When the allowance is full, tool output fails with "no space left on device". Check Avail before a long run, and before you seed worktrees or copy builds.
- Temporary files that the work never deletes fill it. In this repository, they are mostly the parser's folders in `/tmp`. `fortress-repo`'s `references/build-and-caches.md` gives their sweep.
- When it is full, stop your own background processes (`fortress-repo`'s `references/session.md`). Delete what you made and no longer need: scratch, build output, private caches, and finished worktrees whose commits are pushed.
- If that is not enough, commit and push, and report that this session's allowance is spent. A new session starts on a fresh machine.

## The network

Outbound HTTPS goes through the session's proxy, which blocks some hosts. `web.archive.org` resets the connection, and the proxy refuses `labs.oracle.com`.

- If you need a research PDF from these hosts, name it in your report. Only the curator can upload it into the session.
- To read an archived page that is not a PDF, fetch it through the pure.md reader relay: `https://pure.md/https://web.archive.org/web/<timestamp>if_/<url>`. The `if_` after the timestamp is required.

#!/bin/bash
# seed-worktree.sh <base-worktree> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
#
# Makes a worktree that is ready to compile and run Fortress without building anything, by copying the
# build and the caches of a baseline worktree that has been built once, and translating the parts of the
# caches that are keyed by the source tree's absolute path (explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md).
#
#   <base-worktree>  a clean worktree of this repository at some commit B, on which `ant compileAll` and the
#                    library-order recompile (explorations/repo-internals.md, "Compile order matters") have
#                    run, and nothing since.
#   <new-worktree>   where the new worktree goes; made by `git worktree add`, reused if it already exists.
#   <branch>         the branch it checks out: an existing local branch, else origin's, else a new branch
#                    cut from <start-point>, which defaults to B; `-` makes a detached worktree at
#                    <start-point> instead. Old-against-new runs need no copy of the base: tools/old-fortress.sh
#                    runs the base build itself with a private caches folder.
#
# What it does, in order: adds the worktree; copies ProjectFortress/build, ProjectFortress/.dependencies
# and default_repository/caches from the base; renames every file of the AST caches (analyzed_cache,
# interpreter_cache, interpreter_parsed_cache) to the hash of its source's new path (NamingCzar.deCaseName,
# compiler/NamingCzar.java:244-245; GraphNode.java:33 hashes the canonical path) and rewrites the base path
# inside it; rewrites the base path in the bytecode-cache jars' SourceFile attributes (debug information
# only: jars copied unchanged also run, but their stack traces would name the base's files); and makes the
# new worktree the base's replica in its file dates too. The copies keep the base's dates (cp -a), every
# tracked file whose content is the base's takes the base file's date, and every tracked file that differs
# from B, committed or not, is stamped later than everything copied. Dates decide three things. The
# repository uses a cached entry only when it is not older than its source (repository/GraphRepository.java:244,
# :283; a changed api also makes everything that imports it stale, :600-620). Ant regenerates the AST
# nodes, the parsers and Operators.java when an input is newer than the generated file (build.xml:371-384,
# :450-467, :1335-1400); the checkout's own dates make it regenerate them, and javac then recompiles 1,077
# files. And javac recompiles a source newer than its class (build-cache-exploration.md, section 6). So the
# next `fortress compile` of a differing library source rebuilds it, and a worktree whose ProjectFortress/src
# differs from B is seeded with a warning: the copied build is B's, so the worker runs ant compileAll, which
# recompiles the differing sources (and deletes the caches, build.xml:715 and :356), and the library-order
# recompile before its first compiled run. The base's own dates must be a build's: a base built in place by
# ant, or seeded by this script.
#
# A worktree that already has ProjectFortress/build is left alone (a relaunch keeps the worker's own build);
# SEED_FORCE=1 replaces its build and caches with the base's.
#
# Prints one line per step with its time, and the seeded worktree's path last. Exits non-zero, having
# removed nothing, if the base is not built or not clean. Never touches the base or the main tree.
# Run it from anywhere; it needs bash, git, python3, realpath and bc.
set -euo pipefail

BASE_ARG=${1:?usage: seed-worktree.sh <base-worktree> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]}
NEW_ARG=${2:?new worktree path}
BRANCH=${3:?branch}
BASE=$(realpath "$BASE_ARG")
step () { local now; now=$(date +%s.%N); printf '%-34s %5.1f s\n' "$1" "$(echo "$now - $T" | bc)"; T=$now; }
T=$(date +%s.%N); T_START=$T

# The base must be built and clean, or its caches do not describe its commit.
for f in ProjectFortress/build/com/sun/fortress/Shell.class \
         default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar \
         default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar \
         default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/CompilerSystem.jar ; do
    [ -e "$BASE/$f" ] || { echo "seed-worktree: $BASE is not built: $f is missing" >&2 ; exit 2 ; }
done
if [ -n "$(git -C "$BASE" status --porcelain -- ProjectFortress Library default_repository)" ]; then
    echo "seed-worktree: $BASE has changes under ProjectFortress, Library or default_repository:" >&2

(* On the compiled path, a builtinPrimitive body whose string names a static helper of nativeHelpers compiles into a call of that helper, self first for a method. *)
component NativeHelperBindingCompiled
export Executable

less(a:ZZ32, b:ZZ32):Boolean = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intLT")

trait Shape
  same(self, other:Shape):Boolean = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.equality.sEquiv")
  sameAs(other:Shape, self):Boolean = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.equality.sEquiv")
end

object Box(v:ZZ32) extends Shape
  kind():JavaString = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.typeName")
end

add(a:ZZ32, b:ZZ32):ZZ32 = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd")

bazS(s:JavaString):JavaString = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleOverload.baz")
bazI(n:ZZ32):JavaString = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleOverload.baz")

run():() = do
  assert(less(1, 2), "less(1, 2)")
  assert(NOT less(3, 2), "less(3, 2)")
  b = Box(3)
  c = Box(4)
  assert(same(b, b), "same(b, b)")
  assert(NOT same(b, c), "same(b, c)")
  assert(sameAs(b, b), "sameAs(b, b)")
  assert(NOT sameAs(c, b), "sameAs(c, b)")
  assert(b.kind() = "Box", "b.kind()")
  assert(add(2, 3), 5, "add(2, 3)")
  r: ZZ32 := 0
  try
    r := add(2147483647, 1)
  catch e
    IntegerOverflow => r := 1
  end
  assert(r, 1, "add(2147483647, 1) raises IntegerOverflow")
  assert(bazS("x".asJavaString) = "baz x", "bazS")
  assert(bazI(7) = "baz 7", "bazI")
  println("PASS")
end

end
tests=NativeHelperBindingCompiled
link
run
run_out_contains=PASS

content.content:
- **Same name, other meaning.** 25 of B carry a name the compiler prelude binds to another helper. 12 are the wrapping operators: the one library binds `DOTPLUS` to wrapping addition (`FortressLibrary.fss:718`), the compiler prelude to saturating addition (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:676`), ledger row 348. Copying the compiler prelude's binding would be wrong for them.
- **Parameters that are not Java values.** 37 bindings take `AnyIntegral` (17), `Type` (11), `Any` (5), `Number` (3), `T` (3) or a function (4): B 10, C 11, D2 16. The body converts before the call, or the helper takes a Fortress type.
- **The size of C.** 132 distinct glue classes, 0.7K lines of glue Java, median 5 lines each. `RR32` 50 (no float helper exists but `floatToDouble`), `Float` 28 (directed rounding, raw bits, NaN tests), the integer families' `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD`, `LCM`, `partitionL`, `^`, `CHOOSE`, shifts and conversions 42 (the compiler prelude writes the first four in Fortress, `CompilerBuiltin.fss:686-705`), the literals 8, strings and `StringPrim` 10, `nanoTime` 1 (the compiled one returns `RR64`).
- **Every program's output is D1.** `println` writes through `stdOut` (`FortressLibrary.fss:4246-4249`), a native `Writer` object (`Library/Writer.fss:20-24`). The first compiled program on the one library needs `Writer`'s natives.
- **microGPT's path.** It calls `nanoTime` (C) and imports `System` (`explorations/apl/microgpt/MicroGptApl.fss:16`), whose top-level `args` calls `getProgramArgsPrim` (D2) when the component loads (`Library/System.fss:28`). Its arrays reach `NativeArray` (D2).
- **Native objects.** Of the 32, the compiled path has a run-time value class for 12 (`compiler/runtimeValues/`: `FRR64`, `FRR32`, `FFloatLiteral`, `FZZ32`, `FZZ64`, `FNN32`, `FNN64`, `FIntLiteral`, `FZZ`, `FBoolean`, `FCharacter`, `FJavaString`), an analogue for the 5 I/O objects (`FortressBufferedReader`/`Writer`), and nothing for 15 (`Thread`, the 3 arrays, the 11 `Reflect` objects).

### The names

- **The four well-known types.** `Types.STRING`, `JAVASTRING`, `EXCEPTION`, `CHECKED_EXCEPTION` (`compiler/Types.java:66-69`), switched between the apis at `:77-88`. Used outside `Types.java` 5 times: `STRING` at `scala_src/typechecker/impls/Operators.scala:160` and `Misc.scala:461`, `EXCEPTION` at `Misc.scala:741`, `:752`, `:771`; the other two never. The one library declares `String`, `Exception` and `CheckedException` (`FortressLibrary.fsi:2342`, `:1037`, `:1102`) and no `JavaString`. Beside them, `CHARACTER` (`Types.java:65`, used at `Misc.scala:464`) names `Character` where the one library has `Char`: ledger row 477.
- **The foreign-type table.** 15 distinct type names in the builtin api (`NamingCzar.java:337-344`, `:437-450`, `:460-465`). On the one library 5 move to `FortressLibrary` (`ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR64`, `ZZ`, `NN64`), 1 is renamed (`Character` to `Char`), 4 stay (`Boolean`, `RR32`, `NN32`, `IntLiteral`), and 5 have no type (`JavaString`, `JavaBufferedReader`, `JavaBufferedWriter`, `ZZ32Vector`, `StringVector`).
- **Sources that name the prelude.** 43 Java and Scala files, 42 of them in code, 214 lines (`CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra`, `compilerBuiltin()`, `useCompilerLibraries`, `-compiler-lib`):
  - the world switch, 7 files, 48 lines: `Shell.java` 33, `WellKnownNames.java` 9, `Types.java` 2, `NamingCzar.java`, `disambiguator/TopLevelEnv.java`, `linker/Linker.java`, `runtimeSystem/Naming.java` 1 each;
  - the optimizer, the front end and the checker, 6 files, 29 lines: `asmbytecodeoptimizer/Inlining.java` 13, `RemoveLiteralCoercions.java` 6, `codegen/ParallelismAnalyzer.java` 3, `desugarer/IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java` 3, `typechecker/TraitTable.scala` 3, `nodes_util/ExprFactory.java` 1;
  - the run-time value classes, 21 files, 54 lines, `compiler/runtimeValues/` (for example `FZZ32.java:14-15` implements `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.ZZ32`);
  - the helpers, 7 files, 64 lines: the 55 raise strings and the `IntLiteral` helpers;
  - the frozen stub `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/CompilerBuiltin.java`, 19 lines.

## 3. The plan in rungs

The order moves walk onto the helpers first. Walk then runs the same Java as compiled code, so the interpreter suite checks every rebinding the day it lands, long before the compiled path reads the library. The switch-over day is left with the names. The rungs are the same under either answer to the fork below; only the binding form and N0 differ.

#!/bin/bash
# run.sh <tree> <out>: the helper-calls probe's commands, run from a built, seeded tree with a private caches
# folder <out>/caches (copied from <tree>/default_repository/caches). Writes into <out> only:
#   javap-*.txt     the bytecode of the program, of the native wrappers and of the prelude's ZZ32 + chain
#   inline.txt      one run of every loop under -XX:+PrintCompilation -XX:+PrintInlining
#   alloc.tsv       bytes that the program's thread allocates, one JFR run per loop, escape analysis on and off
#   time.txt        one plain run of every loop, each line the loop's result and its nanoseconds
set -euo pipefail
TREE=$(realpath "${1:?usage: run.sh <tree> <out>}"); OUT=$(realpath -m "${2:?out dir}")
HERE=$TREE/explorations/perf-probes/helper-calls
mkdir -p "$OUT"
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
export FORTRESS_HOME=$TREE FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$TREE/tmp FORTRESS_CACHES=$OUT/caches
BASE_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$TREE/tmp"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
[ -d "$OUT/caches" ] || cp -a "$TREE/default_repository/caches" "$OUT/caches"
cd "$HERE"

# 1. compile (about 7 s)
JAVA_FLAGS="$BASE_FLAGS" "$TREE/bin/fortress" compile HelperCalls.fss

# 2. the bytecode
J=$OUT/jar; rm -rf "$J"; mkdir -p "$J/prog" "$J/cb"
(cd "$J/prog" && unzip -q -o "$OUT/caches/bytecode_cache/HelperCalls.jar")
(cd "$J/cb" && unzip -q -o "$OUT/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar" 2>/dev/null || true)
javap -c -p -cp "$J/prog" HelperCalls 'HelperCalls$Shape$DefaultTraitMethods' > "$OUT/javap-HelperCalls.txt"
W=$OUT/caches/nativewrapper_cache
for c in simpleIntArith simpleDoubleArith equality; do
  javap -c -p -cp "$W" native.com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.$c > "$OUT/javap-native-$c.txt"
done
javap -c -p -cp "$J/cb" fortress.CompilerBuiltin 'fortress.CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32$DefaultTraitMethods' \
      'fortress.CompilerBuiltin$RR64$DefaultTraitMethods' > "$OUT/javap-CompilerBuiltin.txt"

# 3. the inlining decisions, every loop in one JVM (about 30 s)
JAVA_FLAGS="$BASE_FLAGS -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintCompilation -XX:+PrintInlining" \
  "$TREE/bin/fortress" run HelperCalls > "$OUT/inline.txt" 2>&1

# 4. allocation per loop, with escape analysis on and off (about 4 minutes)
allocated () {  # the most bytes that one thread of the recording allocated
  jfr print --json --events jdk.ThreadAllocationStatistics "$1" |
    python3 -I -c 'import json,sys; print(max(e["values"]["allocated"] for e in json.load(sys.stdin)["recording"]["events"]))'
}
printf 'loop\tea\tbytes\n' > "$OUT/alloc.tsv"
for ea in on off; do
  [ $ea = on ] && EA=-XX:+DoEscapeAnalysis || EA=-XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis
  for l in none loopLib loopImp loopPre loopLib2 dloopLib dloopImp dloopPre dloopLib2 sameLoop; do
    JAVA_FLAGS="$BASE_FLAGS $EA -Dhelper.loop=$l -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=$OUT/a-$l-$ea.jfr,settings=profile" \
      "$TREE/bin/fortress" run HelperCalls > "$OUT/a-$l-$ea.txt" 2>&1
    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\n' $l $ea "$(allocated "$OUT/a-$l-$ea.jfr")" >> "$OUT/alloc.tsv"
    rm -f "$OUT/a-$l-$ea.jfr"
  done
done

# 5. a plain run of every loop, its own timings (about 30 s)
JAVA_FLAGS="$BASE_FLAGS" "$TREE/bin/fortress" run HelperCalls > "$OUT/time.txt" 2>&1
echo done
EOF

<!-- What the transaction checks cost on the compiled path, measured 2026-10-08 by a delegated worker for the coordinator. Compiled path only; no walk timing. Nothing tracked outside this directory was changed: the checks were removed by a class-path shadow built from inATransaction-false.patch. Command: run.sh beside this file. -->

# What the transaction checks cost on the compiled path

Compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a `MutableFValue` cell. Before each read and each write of the cell, the generated code calls `BaseTask.inATransaction()`. For a local this is in `compiler/codegen/VarCodeGen.java:483-546`, for a field in `:620-726`. This note measures what share of a compiled loop's time these calls take today.

## 1. The answer

Each loop was timed in fresh JVMs, as a pair:
- "with checks" is the tree as it is;
- "without" has the checks removed by a shadow (§ 2).

How to read the table:
- Times are nanoseconds per loop iteration, or per element for TxArray.
- Each time is the median of 15 runs per variant, with the range (min-max) in brackets.
- "Pairs" is the difference inside each pair of runs, taken one after the other.
- All figures are for the third timed loop in each JVM, after the JIT's warm-up.

| program | with checks | without | difference | pairs | share | checks per iteration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TxScalar, the scalar loop | 20.42 (19.28-22.21) | 18.67 (16.42-19.99) | 1.75 | 1.96 (0.11-3.99) | 9 % | 2 |
| TxArray, the array loop | 23.17 (22.07-25.38) | 8.39 (8.17-9.05) | 14.79 | 14.60 (13.75-16.81) | 64 % | 7 |
| TxCell, the bare cell | 17.42 (16.30-19.04) | 14.56 (13.73-19.20) | 2.86 | 2.67 (-2.23-4.63) | 16 % | 2 |

- In the array loop, the checks take about two thirds of the time. Without them the loop runs 2.8 times as fast. The difference is far above the noise: every pair differs by 13.75 ns or more.
- In the scalar loop, the checks take about a tenth of the time. That difference is about as large as the spread between runs.
- One check costs about 2 ns in the array loop (14.79 / 7), and about 1 to 1.5 ns in the two scalar loops.
- The second timed loop shows the same:
  - TxScalar: 22.54 against 20.80 (1.74 ns, 8 %).
  - TxArray: 23.26 against 9.49 (13.77 ns, 59 %).
  - TxCell: 18.55 against 16.48 (2.07 ns, 11 %).
- The first timed loop includes the JIT's warm-up, as the earlier readings' single loops did:
  - TxScalar: 38.40 against 36.02 (2.39 ns, 6 %).
  - TxArray: 26.13 against 12.78 (13.35 ns, 51 %).
  - TxCell: 34.30 against 31.23 (3.07 ns, 9 %).
- Two earlier sessions of the same script, on the same day, agree (third loop; the first session had 7 runs per variant, the second 15):
  - TxScalar: 2.42 ns (11 %) and 3.08 ns (15 %).
  - TxArray: 14.15 ns (63 %) and 14.37 ns (63 %).
  - TxCell: 2.86 ns (16 %) and 3.17 ns (18 %).
- So the scalar loop's share lies between about 9 % and 15 %.

<!-- How the compiled path calls a native helper, probed 2026-10-31 by an Opus worker for the curator's question on the natives' form (P-58): the bytecode of a call of a bound helper, HotSpot's inlining decisions on it, and the bytes each loop allocates, on a small program only (`HelperCalls.fss`), in a worktree seeded from the batch 23 base build (`1f5c49b4f`), removed after; no timing taken, microGPT not run. Commands: run.sh beside this file. -->

# How the compiled path calls a native helper

The question: since climb batch 23 a native binding of the one library may name a static helper of `nativeHelpers/` (P-58; F-298, F-299). Does that form bake in a cost that the JVM cannot remove later?

The answer, in short:

- The code generator does not call the helper. It calls a generated wrapper over the box classes, which unboxes the arguments, calls the helper and boxes the result (section 2).
- When the loop is hot, C2 inlines all of it: the wrapper, the helper, the box's `make` and its constructor chain, and for an operator the dispatcher, the interface call and the trait's body (section 3). The call itself costs nothing in steady state.
- What stays is boxing: one box for each value assigned to a mutable variable, each iteration. Escape analysis removes the other boxes, the temporaries, as long as the box's whole constructor chain inlines (section 4).
- The library's form compiles to the same bytecode as the prelude's own form, byte for byte, and allocates the same (section 5).
- Phase 6 needs no change to the form. The helper's own Java signature, `int intOverflowingAdd(int, int)`, is already the unboxed signature that decision B needs. What phase 6 changes is the calling convention around it (section 6).

## 1. The program and the commands

`HelperCalls.fss` reaches two helpers, `simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd` and `simpleDoubleArith.doubleAdd`, in three forms, each in a hot `while` loop of its own over 20,000,000 iterations, run 5 times:

| loop | form | body of the loop |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `loopLib`, `dloopLib` | the library's: `addLib(a, b) = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd")` | `acc := addLib(acc, 3)` |
| `loopImp`, `dloopImp` | the prelude's: `import java ... {simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd => jAdd}` and `addImp(a, b) = jAdd(a, b)` | `acc := addImp(acc, 3)` |
| `loopPre`, `dloopPre` | the prelude's own binding, `ZZ32`'s and `RR64`'s `+` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:674`, `:938`) | `acc := acc + 3` |
| `loopLib2`, `dloopLib2` | the library's, two calls nested | `acc := addLib(addLib(acc, 1), 2)` |
| `sameLoop` | the library's, in a functional method of a trait, `self` first | `if same(b, b) then k := k + 1 end` |

Each loop also counts `i := i + 1` and tests `i < n`, through the prelude's `ZZ32` operators. The `RR64` loops add a constant `h` held in an immutable local. The property `helper.loop` picks one loop, or `all`.

`run.sh <tree> <out>` runs everything below from a built tree, with a private caches folder `<out>/caches`. It writes the `javap -c` listings, `inline.txt` (every loop under `-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintCompilation -XX:+PrintInlining`), `alloc.tsv` (bytes allocated per loop, from JFR) and `inline-lvl8.txt`. `fortress run` passes `JAVA_FLAGS` to the run's JVM (`bin/run:33-41`).

The machine: 4 CPUs, Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, OpenJDK 25.0.4.1, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, tiered compilation on, `MaxInlineLevel=15`, compact object headers off. Other agents' suites ran beside the probe, at a load of 20 to 25. So the probe takes no timing: the nanoseconds the program prints are not read. Allocated bytes and inlining decisions do not depend on the load.

## 2. What the code generator emits

### A top-level binding

`addLib` (the library's form) and `addImp` (the prelude's form) have the same body, down to the constant-pool entry (`javap -c -p HelperCalls`):

    public static ...FZZ32 addLib(...FZZ32, ...FZZ32);
         2: invokestatic  #51   // Method native/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd:(LFZZ32;LFZZ32;)LFZZ32;
    public static ...FZZ32 addImp(...FZZ32, ...FZZ32);
         2: invokestatic  #51   // Method native/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd:(LFZZ32;LFZZ32;)LFZZ32;

(Package prefixes cut here: `FZZ32` is `com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32`.) `daddLib` and `daddImp` are equal in the same way, at `#62`.

The target is a wrapper class, `native.com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith`, in `nativewrapper_cache/`. Its method unboxes, calls the helper and boxes (`javap -c -p -cp <out>/caches/nativewrapper_cache native.com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith`):

         1: invokevirtual #25   // Method FZZ32.getValue:()I
         5: invokevirtual #25   // Method FZZ32.getValue:()I
         8: invokestatic  #82   // Method com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd:(II)I
        11: invokestatic  #47   // Method FZZ32.make:(I)LFZZ32;

So the answer to the brief's first question is "something else": an `invokestatic` of the wrapper with the boxes, and the wrapper does the unboxing and boxing. `FZZ32.make` and `FRR64.make` allocate a new box each time (`compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32.java:22-24`, `FRR64.java:22`). `FBoolean.make` returns one of two cached objects (`FBoolean.java:24`).

The path in the code:

1. The rewrite turns the body into a call `builtinPrimitive_simpleIntArith_intOverflowingAdd(a, b)` and adds `import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd => builtinPrimitive_simpleIntArith_intOverflowingAdd}` to the component (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java:53-63`, `:111-121`). These are the nodes that a written `import java` and its call give.
2. `ForeignJava` reads the Java class and names each method with the tag `☕` (`repository/ForeignJava.java:514`, `:542`). It has `FortressTransformer` write the wrapper class (`:807`). `FortressMethodAdapter` writes each forwarding method: `getValue` on each argument, `invokestatic` of the helper, `make` on the result (`compiler/nativeInterface/FortressMethodAdapter.java:303-327`, the conversions at `:139-157`).
3. At the call, `CodeGen.forFunctionalRef` maps a `☕`-tagged name to the class `native/<package>/<Class>` (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:3692`, `:3789-3790`; `compiler/NamingCzar.java:1818-1832`). `callStaticSingleOrOverloaded` emits the `invokestatic` with the boxed descriptor (`CodeGen.java:1470-1483`).

A helper that Java overloads gets one wrapper method per overload. The call names the one that the checker chose, by its boxed descriptor: `bazS` and `bazI` of `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` call `simpleOverload.baz:(LFJavaString;)LFJavaString;` and `baz:(LFZZ32;)LFJavaString;`. No dispatcher stands between them. None of the arithmetic helpers is overloaded.

### The prelude's operator

`acc + 3` on `ZZ32` passes through five frames before the helper (`javap -c -p` on `fortress.CompilerBuiltin` and `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32$DefaultTraitMethods`):

1. `CompilerBuiltin."+"(FZZ32, FZZ32)`, the dispatcher: `invokeinterface CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32."+☞0":(LFZZ32;)LFZZ32;`
2. the springboard's instance method `+☞0(FZZ32)`, in `ZZ32$DefaultTraitMethods`, which `FZZ32` extends (`FZZ32.java:14`): `invokestatic "+☞0":(LFZZ32;LFZZ32;)LFZZ32;`
3. the trait's static body, `+☞0(FZZ32, FZZ32)`: `invokestatic native/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd:(LFZZ32;LFZZ32;)LFZZ32;`
4. the wrapper, as above;
5. the helper.

`i < n` takes the same route through a template instance of `CompilerAlgebra`'s `StandardTotalOrder` `<`, to `simpleIntArith.intLT`. A functional method of the program's own trait (`same(self, other: Shape)`) also takes this route: `HelperCalls.same` makes an `invokeinterface` to `Shape."same☞0"`, the springboard's instance method calls its static body, and the static body calls `native/.../equality.sEquiv` with `self` first.

The loop around these calls also boxes each integer literal at each iteration (`FIntLiteral.make(3)`, then `CompilerBuiltin.coerce_ZZ32`), reads and writes each mutable variable through `BaseTask.inATransaction()` and a `MutableFValue` cell, and pushes and pops `FVoid.make()` after each assignment.

## 3. What HotSpot inlines

In every C2 (tier 4) compile of the nine loops, every frame on the helper's path is inlined. This holds both in each loop's first OSR compile and in the compiles that follow its deoptimization. Each loop's first OSR compile was made not entrant by an uncommon trap at about the time the loop first ended, and was compiled again. `loopLib`'s full compile, from `inline.txt` (indentation cut):

    @ 142   HelperCalls::addLib (6 bytes)   inline (hot)
      @ 2   native.com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith::intOverflowingAdd (15 bytes)   inline (hot)
        @ 1   com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32::getValue (5 bytes)   accessor
        @ 8   com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith::intOverflowingAdd (22 bytes)   inline (hot)
        @ 11   com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32::make (9 bytes)   inline (hot)

and its `i + 1`:

    @ 205   fortress.CompilerBuiltin::+ (11 bytes)   inline (hot)
      @ 5   fortress.CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32$DefaultTraitMethods::+☞0 (9 bytes)   inline (hot)
        @ 5   fortress.CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32$DefaultTraitMethods::+☞0 (9 bytes)   inline (hot)
          @ 5   native.com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith::intOverflowingAdd (15 bytes)   inline (hot)

Below each `make`, the constructor chain `FZZ32.<init>`, `ZZ32$DefaultTraitMethods.<init>`, `Number$...`, `Object$...`, `AnyType$Any$...`, `FValue.<init>` and `java.lang.Object.<init>` is inlined too. The interface call inlines with no type guard printed, since `FZZ32` is the only class that implements `ZZ32`.

C2 refuses three calls in these compiles:

- `BaseTask::transaction`, "unloaded signature classes", on the branch for an `atomic` block, which these loops never take;
- `FFloatLiteral::asRR64`, "low call site frequency", for the literal `0.5` before the loop;
- a `StringBuilder` method in `run`.

(Command: list each "failed to inline" line under a `HelperCalls::` compile of `inline.txt`.)

Tier 3, C1's profiling code, is different. There the helper is refused, "callee is too large" (`intOverflowingAdd`, 22 bytes, 22 times), and so is `FValue::<init>`, "inlining too deep" (24 times). C1 inlines only trivial methods beyond 5 frames (`C1InlineStackLimit=5`), and it stops at `C1MaxInlineLevel=9`. Tier-3 code runs only until C2 replaces it.

The depth: counted from the loop, the deepest frame inlined in these loops is at depth 12: the prelude's `+`, then `java.lang.Object.<init>` under the box of its result. For a top-level binding such as `addLib`, the box's `Object.<init>` is at depth 10. At the default `MaxInlineLevel=15`, frames inline down to depth 16 (section 4, last table).

## 4. Where the cost sits

The call costs nothing once C2 has compiled the loop, so what is left to read is allocation. Bytes per iteration are the bytes that the program's thread allocated (JFR's `jdk.ThreadAllocationStatistics`), less a run with no loop (46 MB), divided by 100,000,000 iterations (`alloc.tsv`):

| loop | escape analysis on | escape analysis off | model, on | model, off |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `loopLib` | 32.49 | 112.00 | 32 | 112 |
| `loopImp` | 32.59 | 112.00 | 32 | 112 |
| `loopPre` | 32.50 | 112.00 | 32 | 112 |
| `loopLib2` | 32.76 | 168.00 | 32 | 168 |
| `dloopLib` | 40.41 | 80.00 | 40 | 80 |
| `dloopImp` | 40.95 | 80.00 | 40 | 80 |
| `dloopPre` | 40.43 | 80.00 | 40 | 80 |
| `dloopLib2` | 40.64 | 104.00 | 40 | 104 |
| `sameLoop` | 32.56 | 112.01 | 32 | 112 |

The model counts objects of 16 bytes (`FZZ32`), 24 bytes (`FRR64`) and 24 bytes (`FIntLiteral`), with 12-byte headers.

- With escape analysis off, the numbers fit the model to the byte: each literal's `FIntLiteral` and `FZZ32`, each helper's result, and nothing else. `FBoolean` and `FVoid` are cached.
- With escape analysis on, what stays is one box for each assignment to a mutable variable, each iteration: `acc` and `i`, or `k` and `i`. That is 2 × 16 bytes in the `ZZ32` loops, and 24 + 16 in the `RR64` loops. The rest, within 1 byte per iteration, is the warm-up before C2's code runs.

The one library's 19 `ZZ32` bindings are functional methods of trait `ZZ32`, as the prelude's are. Nothing in the form:

# How the compiled path calls a native helper

The question: since climb batch 23 a native binding of the one library may name a static helper of `nativeHelpers/` (P-58; F-298, F-299). Does that form bake in a cost that the JVM cannot remove later?

The answer, in short:

- The code generator does not call the helper. It calls a generated wrapper over the box classes, which unboxes the arguments, calls the helper and boxes the result (section 2).
- When the loop is hot, C2 inlines all of it: the wrapper, the helper, the box's `make` and its constructor chain, and for an operator the dispatcher, the interface call and the trait's body (section 3). The call itself costs nothing in steady state.
- What stays is boxing: one box for each value assigned to a mutable variable, each iteration. Escape analysis removes the other boxes, the temporaries, as long as the box's whole constructor chain inlines (section 4).
- The library's form compiles to the same bytecode as the prelude's own form, byte for byte, and allocates the same (section 5).
- Phase 6 needs no change to the form. The helper's own Java signature, `int intOverflowingAdd(int, int)`, is already the unboxed signature that decision B needs. What phase 6 changes is the calling convention around it (section 6).

## 1. The program and the commands

`HelperCalls.fss` reaches two helpers, `simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd` and `simpleDoubleArith.doubleAdd`, in three forms, each in a hot `while` loop of its own over 20,000,000 iterations, run 5 times:

| loop | form | body of the loop |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `loopLib`, `dloopLib` | the library's: `addLib(a, b) = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd")` | `acc := addLib(acc, 3)` |
| `loopImp`, `dloopImp` | the prelude's: `import java ... {simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd => jAdd}` and `addImp(a, b) = jAdd(a, b)` | `acc := addImp(acc, 3)` |
| `loopPre`, `dloopPre` | the prelude's own binding, `ZZ32`'s and `RR64`'s `+` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:674`, `:938`) | `acc := acc + 3` |
| `loopLib2`, `dloopLib2` | the library's, two calls nested | `acc := addLib(addLib(acc, 1), 2)` |
| `sameLoop` | the library's, in a functional method of a trait, `self` first | `if same(b, b) then k := k + 1 end` |

Each loop also counts `i := i + 1` and tests `i < n`, through the prelude's `ZZ32` operators. The `RR64` loops add a constant `h` held in an immutable local. The property `helper.loop` picks one loop, or `all`.

`run.sh <tree> <out>` runs everything below from a built tree, with a private caches folder `<out>/caches`. It writes the `javap -c` listings, `inline.txt` (every loop under `-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintCompilation -XX:+PrintInlining`), `alloc.tsv` (bytes allocated per loop, from JFR) and `inline-lvl8.txt`. `fortress run` passes `JAVA_FLAGS` to the run's JVM (`bin/run:33-41`).

The machine: 4 CPUs, Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, OpenJDK 25.0.4.1, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, tiered compilation on, `MaxInlineLevel=15`, compact object headers off. Other agents' suites ran beside the probe, at a load of 20 to 25. So the probe takes no timing: the nanoseconds the program prints are not read. Allocated bytes and inlining decisions do not depend on the load.

## 2. What the code generator emits

         2: invokestatic  #51   // Method native/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd:(LFZZ32;LFZZ32;)LFZZ32;
    public static ...FZZ32 addImp(...FZZ32, ...FZZ32);
         2: invokestatic  #51   // Method native/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd:(LFZZ32;LFZZ32;)LFZZ32;

(Package prefixes cut here: `FZZ32` is `com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32`.) `daddLib` and `daddImp` are equal in the same way, at `#62`.

         5: invokevirtual #25   // Method FZZ32.getValue:()I
         8: invokestatic  #82   // Method com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd:(II)I
        11: invokestatic  #47   // Method FZZ32.make:(I)LFZZ32;

The path in the code:

1. The rewrite turns the body into a call `builtinPrimitive_simpleIntArith_intOverflowingAdd(a, b)` and adds `import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd => builtinPrimitive_simpleIntArith_intOverflowingAdd}` to the component (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java:53-63`, `:111-121`). These are the nodes that a written `import java` and its call give.
2. `ForeignJava` reads the Java class and names each method with the tag `☕` (`repository/ForeignJava.java:514`, `:542`). It has `FortressTransformer` write the wrapper class (`:807`). `FortressMethodAdapter` writes each forwarding method: `getValue` on each argument, `invokestatic` of the helper, `make` on the result (`compiler/nativeInterface/FortressMethodAdapter.java:303-327`, the conversions at `:139-157`).
3. At the call, `CodeGen.forFunctionalRef` maps a `☕`-tagged name to the class `native/<package>/<Class>` (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:3692`, `:3789-3790`; `compiler/NamingCzar.java:1818-1832`). `callStaticSingleOrOverloaded` emits the `invokestatic` with the boxed descriptor (`CodeGen.java:1470-1483`).

A helper that Java overloads gets one wrapper method per overload. The call names the one that the checker chose, by its boxed descriptor: `bazS` and `bazI` of `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` call `simpleOverload.baz:(LFJavaString;)LFJavaString;` and `baz:(LFZZ32;)LFJavaString;`. No dispatcher stands between them. None of the arithmetic helpers is overloaded.

### The prelude's operator

`acc + 3` on `ZZ32` passes through five frames before the helper (`javap -c -p` on `fortress.CompilerBuiltin` and `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32$DefaultTraitMethods`):

1. `CompilerBuiltin."+"(FZZ32, FZZ32)`, the dispatcher: `invokeinterface CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32."+☞0":(LFZZ32;)LFZZ32;`
2. the springboard's instance method `+☞0(FZZ32)`, in `ZZ32$DefaultTraitMethods`, which `FZZ32` extends (`FZZ32.java:14`): `invokestatic "+☞0":(LFZZ32;LFZZ32;)LFZZ32;`
3. the trait's static body, `+☞0(FZZ32, FZZ32)`: `invokestatic native/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd:(LFZZ32;LFZZ32;)LFZZ32;`
4. the wrapper, as above;
5. the helper.

`i < n` takes the same route through a template instance of `CompilerAlgebra`'s `StandardTotalOrder` `<`, to `simpleIntArith.intLT`. A functional method of the program's own trait (`same(self, other: Shape)`) also takes this route: `HelperCalls.same` makes an `invokeinterface` to `Shape."same☞0"`, the springboard's instance method calls its static body, and the static body calls `native/.../equality.sEquiv` with `self` first.

The loop around these calls also boxes each integer literal at each iteration (`FIntLiteral.make(3)`, then `CompilerBuiltin.coerce_ZZ32`), reads and writes each mutable variable through `BaseTask.inATransaction()` and a `MutableFValue` cell, and pushes and pops `FVoid.make()` after each assignment.

      @ 2   native.com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith::intOverflowingAdd (15 bytes)   inline (hot)
        @ 1   com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32::getValue (5 bytes)   accessor
        @ 8   com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith::intOverflowingAdd (22 bytes)   inline (hot)
        @ 11   com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32::make (9 bytes)   inline (hot)

(Command: list each "failed to inline" line under a `HelperCalls::` compile of `inline.txt`.)

# How the compiled path calls a native helper

The question: since climb batch 23 a native binding of the one library may name a static helper of `nativeHelpers/` (P-58; F-298, F-299). Does that form bake in a cost that the JVM cannot remove later?

The answer, in short:

- The code generator does not call the helper. It calls a generated wrapper over the box classes, which unboxes the arguments, calls the helper and boxes the result (section 2).
- When the loop is hot, C2 inlines all of it: the wrapper, the helper, the box's `make` and its constructor chain, and for an operator the dispatcher, the interface call and the trait's body (section 3). The call itself costs nothing in steady state.
- What stays is boxing: one box for each value assigned to a mutable variable, each iteration. Escape analysis removes the other boxes, the temporaries, as long as the box's whole constructor chain inlines (section 4).
- The library's form compiles to the same bytecode as the prelude's own form, byte for byte, and allocates the same (section 5).
- Phase 6 needs no change to the form. The helper's own Java signature, `int intOverflowingAdd(int, int)`, is already the unboxed signature that decision B needs. What phase 6 changes is the calling convention around it (section 6).

## 1. The program and the commands

`HelperCalls.fss` reaches two helpers, `simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd` and `simpleDoubleArith.doubleAdd`, in three forms, each in a hot `while` loop of its own over 20,000,000 iterations, run 5 times:

| loop | form | body of the loop |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `loopLib`, `dloopLib` | the library's: `addLib(a, b) = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd")` | `acc := addLib(acc, 3)` |
| `loopImp`, `dloopImp` | the prelude's: `import java ... {simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd => jAdd}` and `addImp(a, b) = jAdd(a, b)` | `acc := addImp(acc, 3)` |
| `loopPre`, `dloopPre` | the prelude's own binding, `ZZ32`'s and `RR64`'s `+` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:674`, `:938`) | `acc := acc + 3` |
| `loopLib2`, `dloopLib2` | the library's, two calls nested | `acc := addLib(addLib(acc, 1), 2)` |
| `sameLoop` | the library's, in a functional method of a trait, `self` first | `if same(b, b) then k := k + 1 end` |

Each loop also counts `i := i + 1` and tests `i < n`, through the prelude's `ZZ32` operators. The `RR64` loops add a constant `h` held in an immutable local. The property `helper.loop` picks one loop, or `all`.

`run.sh <tree> <out>` runs everything below from a built tree, with a private caches folder `<out>/caches`. It writes the `javap -c` listings, `inline.txt` (every loop under `-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintCompilation -XX:+PrintInlining`), `alloc.tsv` (bytes allocated per loop, from JFR) and `inline-lvl8.txt`. `fortress run` passes `JAVA_FLAGS` to the run's JVM (`bin/run:33-41`).

The machine: 4 CPUs, Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, OpenJDK 25.0.4.1, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, tiered compilation on, `MaxInlineLevel=15`, compact object headers off. Other agents' suites ran beside the probe, at a load of 20 to 25. So the probe takes no timing: the nanoseconds the program prints are not read. Allocated bytes and inlining decisions do not depend on the load.

## 2. What the code generator emits

### A top-level binding

`addLib` (the library's form) and `addImp` (the prelude's form) have the same body, down to the constant-pool entry (`javap -c -p HelperCalls`):

    public static ...FZZ32 addLib(...FZZ32, ...FZZ32);
         2: invokestatic  #51   // Method native/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd:(LFZZ32;LFZZ32;)LFZZ32;
    public static ...FZZ32 addImp(...FZZ32, ...FZZ32);
         2: invokestatic  #51   // Method native/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd:(LFZZ32;LFZZ32;)LFZZ32;

(Package prefixes cut here: `FZZ32` is `com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32`.) `daddLib` and `daddImp` are equal in the same way, at `#62`.

The target is a wrapper class, `native.com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith`, in `nativewrapper_cache/`. Its method unboxes, calls the helper and boxes (`javap -c -p -cp <out>/caches/nativewrapper_cache native.com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith`):

         1: invokevirtual #25   // Method FZZ32.getValue:()I
         5: invokevirtual #25   // Method FZZ32.getValue:()I
         8: invokestatic  #82   // Method com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd:(II)I
        11: invokestatic  #47   // Method FZZ32.make:(I)LFZZ32;

So the answer to the brief's first question is "something else": an `invokestatic` of the wrapper with the boxes, and the wrapper does the unboxing and boxing. `FZZ32.make` and `FRR64.make` allocate a new box each time (`compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32.java:22-24`, `FRR64.java:22`). `FBoolean.make` returns one of two cached objects (`FBoolean.java:24`).

The path in the code:

1. The rewrite turns the body into a call `builtinPrimitive_simpleIntArith_intOverflowingAdd(a, b)` and adds `import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd => builtinPrimitive_simpleIntArith_intOverflowingAdd}` to the component (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java:53-63`, `:111-121`). These are the nodes that a written `import java` and its call give.
2. `ForeignJava` reads the Java class and names each method with the tag `☕` (`repository/ForeignJava.java:514`, `:542`). It has `FortressTransformer` write the wrapper class (`:807`). `FortressMethodAdapter` writes each forwarding method: `getValue` on each argument, `invokestatic` of the helper, `make` on the result (`compiler/nativeInterface/FortressMethodAdapter.java:303-327`, the conversions at `:139-157`).
3. At the call, `CodeGen.forFunctionalRef` maps a `☕`-tagged name to the class `native/<package>/<Class>` (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:3692`, `:3789-3790`; `compiler/NamingCzar.java:1818-1832`). `callStaticSingleOrOverloaded` emits the `invokestatic` with the boxed descriptor (`CodeGen.java:1470-1483`).

A helper that Java overloads gets one wrapper method per overload. The call names the one that the checker chose, by its boxed descriptor: `bazS` and `bazI` of `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` call `simpleOverload.baz:(LFJavaString;)LFJavaString;` and `baz:(LFZZ32;)LFJavaString;`. No dispatcher stands between them. None of the arithmetic helpers is overloaded.

### The prelude's operator

`acc + 3` on `ZZ32` passes through five frames before the helper (`javap -c -p` on `fortress.CompilerBuiltin` and `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32$DefaultTraitMethods`):

1. `CompilerBuiltin."+"(FZZ32, FZZ32)`, the dispatcher: `invokeinterface CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32."+☞0":(LFZZ32;)LFZZ32;`
2. the springboard's instance method `+☞0(FZZ32)`, in `ZZ32$DefaultTraitMethods`, which `FZZ32` extends (`FZZ32.java:14`): `invokestatic "+☞0":(LFZZ32;LFZZ32;)LFZZ32;`
3. the trait's static body, `+☞0(FZZ32, FZZ32)`: `invokestatic native/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd:(LFZZ32;LFZZ32;)LFZZ32;`
4. the wrapper, as above;
5. the helper.

`i < n` takes the same route through a template instance of `CompilerAlgebra`'s `StandardTotalOrder` `<`, to `simpleIntArith.intLT`. A functional method of the program's own trait (`same(self, other: Shape)`) also takes this route: `HelperCalls.same` makes an `invokeinterface` to `Shape."same☞0"`, the springboard's instance method calls its static body, and the static body calls `native/.../equality.sEquiv` with `self` first.

The loop around these calls also boxes each integer literal at each iteration (`FIntLiteral.make(3)`, then `CompilerBuiltin.coerce_ZZ32`), reads and writes each mutable variable through `BaseTask.inATransaction()` and a `MutableFValue` cell, and pushes and pops `FVoid.make()` after each assignment.

## 3. What HotSpot inlines

In every C2 (tier 4) compile of the nine loops, every frame on the helper's path is inlined. This holds both in each loop's first OSR compile and in the compiles that follow its deoptimization. Each loop's first OSR compile was made not entrant by an uncommon trap at about the time the loop first ended, and was compiled again. `loopLib`'s full compile, from `inline.txt` (indentation cut):

    @ 142   HelperCalls::addLib (6 bytes)   inline (hot)
      @ 2   native.com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith::intOverflowingAdd (15 bytes)   inline (hot)
        @ 1   com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32::getValue (5 bytes)   accessor
        @ 8   com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith::intOverflowingAdd (22 bytes)   inline (hot)
        @ 11   com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32::make (9 bytes)   inline (hot)

and its `i + 1`:

    @ 205   fortress.CompilerBuiltin::+ (11 bytes)   inline (hot)
      @ 5   fortress.CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32$DefaultTraitMethods::+☞0 (9 bytes)   inline (hot)
        @ 5   fortress.CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32$DefaultTraitMethods::+☞0 (9 bytes)   inline (hot)
          @ 5   native.com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith::intOverflowingAdd (15 bytes)   inline (hot)

The call costs nothing once C2 has compiled the loop, so what is left to read is allocation. Bytes per iteration are the bytes that the program's thread allocated (JFR's `jdk.ThreadAllocationStatistics`), less a run with no loop (46 MB), divided by 100,000,000 iterations (`alloc.tsv`):

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `loopLib` | 32.49 | 112.00 | 32 | 112 |
| `loopImp` | 32.59 | 112.00 | 32 | 112 |
| `loopPre` | 32.50 | 112.00 | 32 | 112 |
| `loopLib2` | 32.76 | 168.00 | 32 | 168 |
| `dloopLib` | 40.41 | 80.00 | 40 | 80 |
| `dloopImp` | 40.95 | 80.00 | 40 | 80 |
| `dloopPre` | 40.43 | 80.00 | 40 | 80 |
| `dloopLib2` | 40.64 | 104.00 | 40 | 104 |
| `sameLoop` | 32.56 | 112.01 | 32 | 112 |

- With escape analysis off, the numbers fit the model to the byte: each literal's `FIntLiteral` and `FZZ32`, each helper's result, and nothing else. `FBoolean` and `FVoid` are cached.

- Escape analysis removes every temporary box: the literals' boxes, the boxes passed into a wrapper, and in `loopLib2` and `dloopLib2` the inner call's result, which flows straight into the outer helper. Nesting two helpers costs no more than one.
- The prelude's operator (`loopPre`) and the library's binding (`loopLib`) allocate the same.

The removal needs the whole constructor chain under `make` to inline. In `loopLib2`, with C2's depth limit lowered:

| `loopLib2`, escape analysis on | bytes per iteration |
| --- | --- |
| `MaxInlineLevel=15` (the default) | 32.76 |
| `MaxInlineLevel=9` | 33.19 |
| `MaxInlineLevel=8` | 96.24 |

At 8, C2 refuses `java.lang.Object::<init>` (10 times) and `AnyType$Any$DefaultTraitMethods::<init>` (twice), "inlining too deep" (`inline-lvl8.txt`). From then on, the temporaries whose chain passes depth 9 stay allocated: 96 = 168 less the three `FIntLiteral`s, whose chain is shorter. So a frame at depth d inlines when d ≤ `MaxInlineLevel` + 1.

So the cost sits in the boxing, not in the call. One box is allocated per value that a mutable variable holds across an iteration, and the transaction checks around each read and write of the variable come with it. This agrees with the earlier readings: boxing as the main representational cost (F-11), and boxing, the transaction check and a call per element as a loop's cost (F-40; `perf-probes/transactions/REPORT.md`). Once C2 has compiled the loop, no part of it is the native's call.

The headroom is not large. The prelude's operator reaches depth 12, against the 16 at which inlining stops. By reading, the switch-over takes 2 of those 4 frames, if `FZZ32` extends the one library's `ZZ32` springboard as it extends the prelude's today (`FZZ32.java:14`).
